Question: Is light considered more of a particle or a wave? What evidence do scientists use to support their belief?
Answer: Light, like all other “quantum” entities, can manifest either wave like or particle like behavior. Of course, you have no idea what it’s doing unless you make some kind of measurement / observation. Whether you observe wave like or particle like behavior just depends on the details of your experiment and how exactly you are interacting with the light. This isn’t really an “all or nothing” thing - it’s not like light has a “mode switch” that flips it into either “particle behavior” or “wave behavior.” Light just does what it does. The particle or wave attribution comes from how we interpret what we see when we observe the light. If we do Young’s original double slit experiment and see an interference pattern, we think of that as wave like behavior. Then, if we gradually reduce the intensity of the light that pattern begins to become dimmer, and eventually instead of seeing a smooth continuous pattern we’ll begin to see intermittent flashes of light on the display screen, showing up at random intervals. They show up more often where the interference pattern was bright, and less often where it was dim. We think of those individual, very localized flashes as “particle like behavior.” Of course, the original bright interference pattern was made of localized flashes too - there were just so many of them that they blurred together and we couldn’t discern them anymore. So you still have the wavelike behavior of the interference pattern, but along with it you have the particle like behavior of individual localized flashes. You can see both behaviors at the same time. It’s very important to remember than how you engage with the light is critically important to what you observe. The whole point of quantum theory - the big thing that distinguishes it from classical theory, is that in classical theory we tacitly assume that if our technology is good enough then we can reduce the influence we have on the system we’re studying as much as we want to - we can make the “perturbation” we create on the system’s behavior negligibly small if we want to. But quantum theory acknowledges that this is not true - that there is a minimum influence we can have on the system if we interact with it at all, and if that is enough to affect it significantly, then there’s nothing we can do about that. This is probably the most important aspect of quantum theory to understand. Stay safe and well! Question: What is the purpose of a GPS receiver syncing with satellites' signals, specifically code phase and time offset?
Answer: Think a little about how you might use communication with a constellation of satellites to determine your position on Earth. Basically, you are triangulating. One way or another you can determine where all the satellites are, and by measuring the time offset you can determine how far away they are. With several satellites in play, all of them specific distances away, there will only be one place you could be that would result in those particular time offsets. That’s the gist of how it works - the rest is just the math (arithmetic really) needed to solve for the position. Imagine that Alice is in one corner of your room and you know you are 10 feet from her. You could draw a 10 foot radius circle around her, and you might be anywhere on that circle. Now Bob is in another corner, and you are 12 feet from him. You can draw a 12 foot circle around him, and you’re on that circle too. Those circles might cross in two places. If you have a third person in another corner, you can determine which crossing point you’re at. Obviously GPS works in 3D instead of 2D, but it’s the same idea. Takes more satellites because of the extra dimension. Stay safe and well! Kip ____________________ If you enjoy my answers, please consider supporting my work at Kip Ingram's Space.

Question: Can you explain how Einstein's theory of relativity challenges the concept of absolute space and time? What is the significance of this idea?
Answer: It’s a simple idea. There is no way to identify any point in space as “special” in any way. The only way you can talk about places is in relation to other places (25 miles north of <blah>, etc.) Space just doesn’t come with a built in set of special labels - we can use any labeling system we want and we just choose where our origin will be and what directions our axes will point and so on. And the laws of physics do not care how we make that choice. As long as we solve our problems in correct ways we’ll get the right answers, regardless. It also doesn’t matter whether the coordinate system is moving. I can pick a coordinate system and do a set of experiments to figure out the laws of physics. You can choose a coordinate system that’s moving at some fixed speed relative to mine, and you can do your experiments and you’ll get the same laws of physics. If there were only you in the universe you’d have no way whatsoever to talk about where you were, or whether you were moving or not, etc. All of these things are defined only with respect to other objects. Question: Will the strength of a magnet's power differ after a year of isolation compared to a year of satisfied/unsatisfied attraction to or repulsion from another or just floating alone in space?
Answer: Magnets change over time due to temperature related effects. The higher the magnet’s temperature, the more random thermal agitation you have inside the thing. This agitation is constantly trying to “jiggle around” the magnetic domains - to throw them out of magnetic alignment. If it succeeds completely in doing so, the material will no longer have an self-produced magnetic field. On the other hand, the magnetized state is a state of lower energy, and so that’s the state the material “wants” to be in - it’s like a ball wanting to sit in the bottom of a bowl. There is a natural tendency toward alignment. These two effects compete, with heat trying to undo the magnetism and energy considerations trying to re-magnetize the material. What the steady state result is depends on the details. So, if the magnet is initially away from the long-term equilibrium state, then it will change over time. If it’s already in equilibrium to start with, then it won’t. If you change the temperature, the equilibrium point will change and you’ll get some alteration over time. Etc. Stay safe and well!
